newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish flood relief effort gains pace.
newsitem.headline: Polish flood relief effort gains pace.

text.p: Poland mustered funds for a huge reconstruction effort on Monday as flood waters receded in some worst-hit areas, while continuing to threaten other communities along the raging Odra river.

Finance Minister Marek Belka said he planned cuts in budget spending to cover reconstruction and saw a possible $300 million soft loan from the World Bank to fight a calamity so great that Poland has called a day of mourning for Friday. Thirty-six have died.
"We have quite a lot of funds," said
A week of downpours inundated large areas of south Poland as well as the neighbouring Czech Republic and sent surges of high water rolling north along major rivers, especially the Odra.

The city of Wroclaw was slowly emerging from water after its citizens mounted a largely-successful sandbag defence of the historic centre, with its churches and precious library. But the Odra swamped most of their city at the weekend. @
Villages near Legnica and the fine town of Glogow, partly restored from World War Two devastation, were next in line.
A less dangerous swell on the Wisla river reached Warsaw on Monday without spilling over or seriously harming the capital.
The government picked national labour office chief Andrzej Pilat to oversee long-term reconstruction.
"He is being given unprecedented powers as the situation is so extraordinary," cabinet office head Grzegorz Rydlewski said.
The official crisis committee said 1,200 sq kms of Poland still lay under water, while floods had covered a total of 4,000, PAP news agency reported. @
Parliament will return from recess for a special sitting on Wednesday to amend two dozen laws, including this year's budget, partly to allow higher borrowing to repair damage.
Some opposition chiefs challenged the cabinet decision not to declare an emergency, a move which could have helped relief efforts but would have delayed elections set for September 21.
"The Union for Freedom is concerned...that a state of emergency was not declared in connection with the disaster," a party leader, Bronislaw Geremek, told a news conference. @
It was one of many reproaches flung at the government, led by ex-communists, which faces a strong challenge from a rightist alliance at the parliamentary polls.
Questions arose as to whether Wroclaw's 650,000 people could have been spared if authorities had blasted gaps in dykes upstream of the city, to free water into the countryside. @

Wroclaw council's deputy president, Stanislaw Huskowski, told Gazeta Wyborcza daily that uninsured local villagers, who stopped engineers from blowing the dykes, were desperate after the government had said there would be no compensation.
He estimated the costs of compensating villagers would have been a tenth of those for damage to the city.

Where floods receded, dozens of towns and hundreds of villages were left strewn with sewage and dead cattle. Officials warned the hundreds of thousands of flood victims to clean everything at home and sterilise drinking water. @
The effects of the flood bit on the Warsaw stock exchange, which fell overall. Trading in seven firms has been suspended following losses due to flood damage.
